claims.statement: Feature 073 provides per-user scheduled and on-demand backups of movie collections to user-owned S3-compatible or WebDAV storage, with versioning, keep-last-N retention, and restore that only ever creates a new collection.

Destination credentials (S3 secret key, WebDAV app password) are sealed and never returned/logged/echoed; a destination probe failure can only report which kind of failure occurred, never the server's actual reply, and account deletion does not delete the user's stored backup artifacts because they belong to the user's own storage.

An unattended scheduled backup run acts as the user via a Keycloak offline token granted through explicit consent; there is no service account or privileged fallback, so a revoked or missing grant makes the run fail rather than use another identity.

The BFF's MongoDB is a standalone mongod with no replica set and no multi-document transactions, so exactly-once job scheduling rests on a single-document atomic claim (findOneAndUpdate) rather than a transaction; the Redis leader lock beside it is an optimization with a TTL guess, not the correctness guarantee.

BACKUP_MAX_MOVIES and BACKUP_MAX_UNCOMPRESSED_BYTES exist because a backup run holds the entire artifact in memory instead of streaming it: the runner builds the whole artifact, checks both ceilings in their independent units (count and uncompressed bytes) BEFORE anything is written, and PUTs it as one object, so a failure can never leave a partial object that the user later discovers is unrestorable at the moment they need it; the ceilings are what make that trade defensible and they fail loudly, naming both the limit and the measured value, with streaming snapshots a deliberate filed follow-up rather than an oversight.

The scheduler tick is server.js POSTing to the internal /bff-api/backups/tick route over loopback (127.0.0.1) with a shared secret, because server.js is CommonJS outside the Metro bundle and cannot import src/bff-server/* directly; consequently no tick fires under `pnpm start` in dev and the tick route must be called directly.

Retention's safety property is that a failed or partial run prunes nothing, and a prune failure never fails the run — it is recorded separately in pruneFailureReason distinct from the run's failureReason.

Revocation ordering on disabling a schedule, deleting a job, or deleting the account is revoke-at-Keycloak-first, forget-locally-second, so a failed revocation never strands a live non-expiring offline token with no local record pointing at it.

The audit-sink redaction rule strips any key containing 'token' plus an explicit redact list, which does not name secretEnc, accessKeyId, or a destination password by field name; those fields are excluded by construction rather than by the token-matching rule and are asserted against real secret values in backup-audit.integration.test.ts.

Feature 076 added an account-deletion route (GET/POST /bff-api/account/delete, reachable only after a Keycloak step-up re-authentication) whose runAccountDeletion pipeline in account-deletion.ts calls tearDownUserBackups(userId) as its first step, before deleteCollections, removeAgentConfig, clearTransientState, terminateSessions, logoutIdpSessions, and deleteIdentity (deleteUser in keycloak.ts, always last); account-deletion-order.test.ts pins this step order.

Streaming snapshots are not implemented (the size/count ceiling stands in for them), and failure notification is in-app only with no outbound email channel, since the existing email service only drives Keycloak account flows.

tearDownUserBackups (backup-offline-token.ts) revokes the user's backup offline token at Keycloak first, throwing and deleting nothing locally if revocation fails, and only then deletes the user's backup destinations, jobs, and run history in that order; it never deletes the artifacts already stored at the user's own S3/WebDAV destination, since account-deletion.ts never imports the destination driver or retention modules, a fact pinned by account-deletion-no-driver.test.ts.

runAccountDeletion throws on the first failing step and runs nothing after it, so a partially failed deletion leaves the account intact and reportable as not-deleted; a retry restarts from tearDownUserBackups, and because that step revokes the offline token before any local deletion, a run in flight when its owner is deleted loses its permission and fails rather than retrying (spec FR-034).

Since feature 083 (#702) the scheduled-backup consent round trip runs as its own Keycloak client (BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_ID, mcm-backup-consent) rather than the login client, because Keycloak answers the consent request from the member's existing SSO session and attaches the offline grant to it: revoking a grant issued to the login client removes that client from the session, so the member's still-locally-valid access token can no longer be exchanged for an agent subject token (invalid_token, the assistant answers "No caller identity") and the next refresh fails with 'Session not active', signing them out. Measured on Keycloak 26.8.0; prompt=login and admin-API offline-session deletion do not avoid it, and a grant issued to a separate client detaches only that client.

The app-e2e signature of the #702 defect is not flake: in every app-e2e run where the BFF logged 'Agent subject-token exchange failed', the BFF had logged backup_schedule_consent_revoked 2 min 10 s – 2 min 45 s earlier, which is one failed attempt's 150 s timeout followed by the retry, and the same mechanism is a production defect because disabling a last schedule, deleting its job, or an account teardown revokes the grant.

A stored backup grant is always used and revoked as the client it was issued to, read from the refresh token's azp claim (credentialsFor), so grants minted by the login client before feature 083 keep working with no migration of stored data; an azp matching neither client falls back to the login identity, which Keycloak then refuses, so the grant fails as unusable instead of being presented with a secret that does not belong to it.

With BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_ID unset the BFF falls back to the login client — reproducing the defect above — and logs backup_consent_shared_client once; BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_SECRET is optional and defaults to the login client's secret because the BFF is the only custodian of both.

The backup-consent callback URI must be registered on the dedicated consent client as well as the login client, because Keycloak refuses an authorize request naming an unregistered redirect URI; /bff-api/auth/init makes a second ensureClientRedirectUris call for the consent client whenever the configured consent client differs from the login client, and an integration test pins that the pre-existing login-client URIs survive the call.

The dedicated consent client must already exist in a realm before BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_ID is set: CI imports ci-realm.json fresh every run so the client is always present there and gen-ci-env.mjs sets the variable, but an existing dev or production realm is imported IGNORE_EXISTING and does not gain the client from the realm JSON, so setting the variable first breaks consent with 'client not found' and the operator must create the client in the running realm first.

The backup destination URL guard is the inverse of the Ollama SSRF guard in policy: loopback, RFC 1918, link-local (including the cloud-metadata address), carrier-grade-NAT/tailnet and other non-public addresses are denied by default and admitted only when the host is named on BACKUP_ALLOWED_DESTINATION_HOSTS, and an unresolvable name is treated as unsafe rather than as nothing blocked being found.

The destination check runs on save, on every probe and on every use, and it resolves all DNS answers rather than the first and pins the outbound connection to the vetted address set — so a hostname that was safe when saved but later resolves into private space cannot be written to, and the address checked is the address connected to.

The offline standing permission is given up only when no enabled job carrying a schedule remains for the user (revokeIfNoScheduleRemains counts remaining jobs before revoking), not on the first disable, so disabling one job does not silently break the user's other schedules.

In production the backup feature is switched on entirely from the prod-mcm-bff stack block in infrastructure-as-code/komodo/stacks.toml rather than the Komodo UI, which the next ResourceSync overwrites: that block supplies BACKUP_CREDENTIAL_ENC_KEY and BACKUP_TICK_SECRET (masked Komodo Variables) and BACKUP_ALLOWED_DESTINATION_HOSTS (plain, since it is LAN topology) plus BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_ID and the Variable behind BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_SECRET; each Variable must exist before the sync that first references it or Komodo writes the literal placeholder, and a sync changing only the environment does not recreate the container so a Redeploy is required. Until 2026-10-25 none of the three switches was set, so backups were off in production — the symptoms were 'That address is not allowed' on a LAN destination and 'backup scheduler disabled' at boot (item #843, spec 083 T009).
The dev and CI environment generators seed BACKUP_CREDENTIAL_ENC_KEY rather than syncing it, because rewriting the key on a re-run would orphan every stored destination secret and offline token.

The tick route refuses a wrong or missing secret by answering 404 rather than 401, so the route does not advertise itself, and it compares the presented header in constant time with a length pre-check that falls through to the same 404; a supplied ?now= instant is refused with 400 unless BACKUP_TICK_ALLOW_TIME_OVERRIDE=1 (dev and CI only), and 'leader: false' is a normal 200 because another instance legitimately took the lock.

In production the dedicated backup-consent Keycloak client is created through the admin console rather than the runbook's kcadm.sh block, because the bootstrap admin is retired and the named admins have 2FA, which a kcadm password login cannot satisfy; the console cannot reuse the login client's secret, so the client gets its own, held as the masked Komodo Variable that BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_SECRET references. The committed prod-realm.json template does define the client, but only for a fresh install, and it carries no secret value.

The offline standing permission is stored inside the user's agent-config document as offlineRefreshEnc, which is why the account-deletion pipeline must run tearDownUserBackups before removeAgentConfig: deleting that document first would destroy the only local record of a token still live at Keycloak, leaving nothing in the system that knows it exists.

The BACKUP_ALLOWED_DESTINATION_HOSTS allow-list is compared as an exact lower-cased host match with no port, never a substring or suffix test, because a suffix test would admit a name such as nas.home.arpa.attacker.test to an allow-list entry of nas.home.arpa — the classic way an allow-list becomes a vulnerability instead of a control.

The feature-073 backup integration suites SKIP rather than fail when the two real backup destinations are absent, so they must be run with MCM_REQUIRE_BACKUP_TARGETS=1 alongside MCM_REQUIRE_LIVE_STACK=1: the flag converts the skip into a hard failure that names the missing input, and the jest global preflight then also probes Backup S3's /health/ready and the WebDAV endpoint's unauthenticated 401 — which is the only place the distroless WebDAV container's liveness is asserted.

Retention only ever treats keys matching `<basePath>/<jobId>/<iso>.json.gz` as deletion candidates, filtered both by the job prefix and by an artifact-name check, so another job's objects and any file the user keeps at the same destination — including one inside this job's own folder — are never deleted.

Destination secrets and offline grants are sealed under the feature's own AES-256-GCM master key BACKUP_CREDENTIAL_ENC_KEY, deliberately separate from AGENT_CONFIG_ENC_KEY so that key's blast radius is not widened from the user's assistant credentials to every store the user's whole collection can be written to; the key is read at first use rather than at boot so a deployment that configures no destination still starts, and rotating it makes every stored destination secret and offline token unreadable, forcing each user to re-enter their destination and grant consent again.

Backup encrypted blobs are bound by AAD to their owner and field, so a store-layer mixup fails the GCM authentication check loudly instead of decrypting: a destination secret is bound to userId plus destinationId (not userId alone, which would make two of one user's own destination secrets interchangeable), while the offline grant is bound to userId alone because a user consents once and revocation is a single act.

Granting backup consent also requires the realm's offline_access role, which Keycloak reaches through the realm's default-roles composite: a user created through the Admin API inherits it, but a user created by a realm-JSON import gets it only if that import grants the default role, and the failure is invisible — it surfaces as a blank page after sign-in rather than an error, which is how the seeded e2e-test-user once ended up unable to consent.

The scheduling tick is silent when nothing is due, by design, so its liveness proof is the first Mongo connect one interval after boot rather than a per-tick log line; a job that never runs usually has no nextRunAt at all, because a disabled job deliberately carries none so that re-enabling does not fire for an occurrence that passed while it was off, and a job left claimed by an instance that died self-heals after the 30-minute reclaim ceiling. Catch-up is deliberately once-only: a job whose time passed while the system was down is claimed once on recovery with its next occurrence computed forward from now, since advancing occurrence by occurrence would fire repeatedly and, with keep-last retention, prune away the history the downtime was meant to preserve.

Revoking the standing permission through the consent route also switches every one of the user's remaining schedules off, and only after the revocation itself has succeeded — a schedule left on could only ever produce a failed run, and the settings screen would report backups off over a switch still reading On. The jobs themselves are kept: they still run on demand and still own the versions at the destination.

The web E2E backups spec skips rather than fails when the backup destinations are absent (it gates on BACKUP_TEST_S3_SECRET_KEY being set) and escalates through its own flag E2E_REQUIRE_BACKUP_TARGETS=1, which the app-e2e Playwright invocation sets, rather than through MCM_REQUIRE_BACKUP_TARGETS; locally the values it needs — BACKUP_TICK_SECRET and the BACKUP_TEST_* credentials — live in .env.local, which Playwright does not load (loadE2eEnv reads only .env.e2e.local), so they must be passed explicitly, since supplying only the e2e env file once produced a green run whose backup specs had silently skipped; in CI they are not read from a file at all — the app-e2e bring-up step mints the S3/WebDAV credentials per run and exports them through $GITHUB_ENV, and it reads BACKUP_TICK_SECRET back out of the generated .env.docker rather than minting a second value, because a second random secret is just as valid-looking and would 404 against the BFF holding the first.
